description: Contact Center configuration tables, in write order. The manifest says which tables move, in which stage, and how a record is recognised in another environment (matchKeys). Columns and lookups are NOT listed here: the engine reads them from each environment's metadata, compares and writes every writable setting except the exclusions below, and links lookups that point at a later table in a final pass. move: upsert | create-once (never update) | update-only (never create) | reference (read to resolve lookups, never compared or written) | detect (report only).

stages.label: Foundations
stages.description: Operating hours, skills, rating models, capacity profiles and templates

stages.label: Workstream details
stages.description: Capacity profiles per workstream and context variables

stages.label: Decision contracts
stages.description: Inputs and outputs that rulesets work on

stages.label: Routing and assignment
stages.description: Routing configurations, assignment methods and their steps

stages.label: Channels
stages.description: Live chat, voice, SMS and WhatsApp settings

stages.label: Conversation orchestration
stages.description: Playbooks and the prompts that drive them

stages.label: Agent scripts
stages.description: The scripts agents follow during a conversation, and their steps

tables.label: Languages
tables.notes: System reference data. Channels point at a language; the lookup is mapped by locale ID.

tables.label: Chat widget languages
tables.notes: System reference data for the live chat widget locale.

tables.label: Record routing hubs
tables.notes: One per table that has record routing (Case routing hub for incident). A record workstream (email, case) must point at its table's hub, so the lookup is mapped by table name. Set up record routing for that table in the target first; its intake rules are not moved.

tables.label: Orchestration scenarios
tables.notes: The scenarios a conversation orchestration playbook is built on ('Escalate priority based on transfer to a queue'). They ship with the product, identically in every environment, so they are mapped, never written. Two of the 28 share a name; a playbook built on that one is reported ambiguous.

tables.label: Operating hours
tables.notes: The calendar behind the hours is a separate record per environment; set the working hours again in the target after a create.

tables.label: Skills
tables.notes: Referenced by rulesets and agents.

tables.label: Rating models
tables.notes: Skill proficiency scale. Written before its rating values.

tables.label: Rating values
tables.notes: A rating value is only unique within its rating model.

tables.label: Capacity profiles
tables.notes: Shared across workstreams.

tables.label: Notification templates
tables.notes: Matched on unique name: workstreams refer to their templates by unique name.

tables.label: Session templates
tables.notes: Matched on unique name: workstreams refer to their templates by unique name, and display names are not unique.

tables.label: Workstreams
tables.notes: Creating a workstream starts provisioning in Dataverse; the run waits for it. Its default queue and routing contract are linked after queues and contracts are written.

tables.label: Workstream capacity
tables.notes: Which capacity profiles a workstream uses. Both sides must exist first.

tables.label: Context variables
tables.notes: Rulesets read these, so they exist before rulesets are written.

tables.label: Queues
tables.notes: Only unified routing queues; personal and system queues are left out. Queue members are not copied. Overflow rulesets and the assignment contract are linked after they are written.

tables.label: Decision contracts
tables.notes: Created when missing, never changed: rulesets depend on their exact shape.

tables.label: Rulesets
tables.notes: The definition embeds the GUIDs of queues, skills and workstreams; they are rewritten to the target's. Written twice so Dataverse records its dependencies.

tables.label: Routing configurations
tables.notes: Every workstream gets its own 'Contact center routing configuration', so the workstream is part of the key.

tables.label: Routing steps
tables.notes: Steps such as classification and route-to-queue, under their routing configuration. The admin center often gives a configuration's classification and route-to-queue steps the same name, so the step type is part of the key; classification steps with one name are told apart by step order.

tables.label: Assignment methods
tables.notes: Custom assignment methods belong to a queue.

tables.label: Assignment steps
tables.notes: Prioritization and assignment rules under an assignment method.

tables.label: Live chat widgets
tables.notes: The widget snippet and app ID are generated per environment and stay as they are.

tables.label: Voice channels
tables.notes: Phone numbers are acquired per environment and are not copied.

tables.label: SMS channels
tables.notes: Needs its phone number in the target before it can be created; settings of an existing one are updated.

tables.label: Custom channels
tables.notes: A custom messaging (Messaging API) channel on its workstream. Creating one needs a managed identity and bot registration set up per environment in the admin center; the settings of an existing one are updated.

tables.label: WhatsApp channels
tables.notes: Needs its WhatsApp account in the target before it can be created; settings of an existing one are updated.

tables.label: Quick replies
tables.notes: A quick reply is unique per title and language.

tables.label: Tags
tables.notes: Free-standing.

tables.label: Contact center settings
tables.notes: One per environment and always present, so it is only ever updated.

tables.label: Playbooks
tables.notes: Conversation orchestration playbooks (preview). This is the header: which scenario it is built on, which event triggers it, and whether it runs rule-based or through a language model. The instruction itself is in the prompt underneath it.

tables.label: Playbook prompts
tables.notes: The natural-language instruction under a playbook, with the queues it applies to. The compiled rule (msdyn_workflowrule, a file) is left behind on purpose: publishing in the target regenerates it from this prompt, so what moves is the authored intent and not a compiled rule pointing at another environment's queues. The queue lists are read as references, so queues are remapped like everywhere else. A moved playbook arrives at the stage it had in the source; publishing it stays a step someone takes in the target.

tables.label: Agent scripts
tables.notes: A script an agent follows during a conversation. The unique name is what the product keys it on, so that is what it is matched on here.

tables.label: Agent script steps
tables.notes: The steps under a script, in order. A step that routes to another script has that script remapped like any other lookup. A step that runs a macro is reported instead: see detectOnly.

detectOnly.message: Runs a macro. A macro is a solution component, not configuration data: move it by solution, then pick it on the step in the target.
Uses a phone number. Acquire a number in the target environment and assign it to this channel.
Uses an SMS number. Add the number in the target environment before this channel can be created.
Uses a Copilot Studio agent. Move the agent by solution, then pick it on the workstream in the target.
Uses a WhatsApp account. Connect the account in the target environment before this channel can be created.
